assumptions_latex: The node problem is polynomial optimization on a compact basic semialgebraic set.
A selected moment–SOS relaxation order \(d\) is feasible and has value \(\rho_d\).
The surrounding conic architecture already maintains a valid lower bound \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The imported bound \(L^+:=\max\{L,\rho_d\}\) remains valid for the node optimum \(p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface statement imports one selected SDP bound, not the underlying positivity hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*\) be the minimum of a polynomial node problem and let \(\rho_d\) be the optimal value of a selected order-\(d\) moment–SOS semidefinite relaxation. The interface exports the scalar inequality \(\rho_d\le p^*\), together with any solver certificate needed to validate that inequality, to the surrounding conic relaxation system. If that system currently has lower bound \(L\le p^*\), its combined bound is represented by \[L^+:=\max\{L,\rho_d\}\le p^*.\] No moment matrix, positivity representation, convergence assertion, or minimizer-extraction rule is duplicated by this interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected moment–SOS SDP contributes its certified scalar lower bound to the conic architecture, which combines it with existing bounds by taking their maximum.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment–SOS Relaxation Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar-bound interface matches the leaf role and representation is an appropriate content kind. A source with a specific locator is required for the moment–SOS lower-bound convention and certificate interface.

assumptions_latex: The minimization problem has feasible set \(F\) and linear objective \(c^\top x\).
The conic relaxation has closed convex feasible region \(R\supseteq F\).
The relaxation attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(F)\), then \(\min_{x\in R}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x\) for every \(c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness is stated for linear optimization through convex-hull equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic relaxation region \(R\) is exact for all linear objectives on \(F\) when it represents the closed convex hull of the original feasible set: \[R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(F).\] Under this equality, every vector \(c\) satisfies \[\min_{x\in R}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x.\] For a fixed objective \(c\), objective-specific exactness requires only equality of these two values; it does not imply equality of \(R\) and \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(F)\). Thus hull exactness is the objective-uniform regime, whereas value equality is the weaker instance-specific regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic relaxation is uniformly exact when its feasible region equals the closed convex hull of the original feasible set; fixed-objective exactness only requires equal optimal values.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Conic Relaxation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between objective-uniform hull exactness and fixed-objective value exactness is precise, and condition fits the container. No source is cited for this characterization.

assumptions_latex: Every semidefinite block has arrow form with scalar \(t\) and vector \(u\).
All remaining constraints and the objective use only the shared variables \((t,u,z)\).
No additional constraint uses unrepresented entries of the semidefinite block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The SOC and SDP formulations have identical projections and therefore identical feasible sets and optimal values in the shared variables.

notation.meaning: arrow matrix representing one SOC constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence through the standard arrow-matrix representation of a Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), define \[M(t,u):=\begin{pmatrix}t&u^\top\\u&tI_n\end{pmatrix}.\] The equivalence \[\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M(t,u)\succeq0\] identifies the Lorentz-cone constraint with an arrow-structured semidefinite constraint. Consequently, if every SDP block in a relaxation has this form and no constraint or objective depends on additional matrix entries, projecting the SDP formulation onto the shared variables \((t,u,z)\) yields exactly the SOC formulation. The two relaxations then have the same feasible projection, infeasibility status, and optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDP relaxation is equivalent to an SOC relaxation when all PSD blocks are standard arrow representations and no model component uses additional matrix entries.
knowledge_statements.title: SOC–SDP Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arrow-matrix equivalence and projection qualification are mathematically consistent, and representation fits the leaf. A specifically located conic-optimization source is required.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation regions \(R_s\) and \(R_w\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
The stronger region satisfies \(R_s\subsetneq R_w\).
Both relaxations minimize a linear objective over the same ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(c\) such that \(\min_{x\in R_s}c^\top x>\min_{x\in R_w}c^\top x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict dominance is distinguished from mere containment by an objective-value separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_s\subsetneq R_w\) be nonempty compact convex relaxation regions for a minimization problem. Then the strong relaxation dominates the weak one: for every linear objective \(c\), \[L_s(c):=\min_{x\in R_s}c^\top x\ge L_w(c):=\min_{x\in R_w}c^\top x.\] Moreover, strict inclusion implies that some linear objective separates the regions and satisfies \[L_s(c)>L_w(c).\] For a prescribed objective, strict relaxation dominance occurs precisely when this latter inequality holds; strict feasible-set inclusion alone does not force a strict bound for every objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested compact convex relaxations give ordered lower bounds. Strict inclusion guarantees a strict gap for some linear objective, but not necessarily for the model’s particular objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Relaxation-Dominance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For nonempty compact convex regions, the stated dominance and existence of a separating linear objective are correct; property fits the container. The claim has no cited source or locator.

assumptions_latex: The compact node domains satisfy \(D_{k+1}\subseteq D_k\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(D_k)\to0\).
Each relaxation underestimator \(\ell_k\) obeys \(\ell_k(x)\le f(x)\) on \(D_k\).
There is a modulus \(\omega\) with \(\omega(t)\to0\) and \(0\le f(x)-\ell_k(x)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}(D_k))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The node relaxation gap satisfies \(0\le p_k-L_k\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}(D_k))\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic tightness follows from uniform relaxation consistency on shrinking compact domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each compact node domain \(D_k\), define \(p_k:=\inf_{x\in D_k}f(x)\) and \(L_k:=\inf_{x\in D_k}\ell_k(x)\), where \(\ell_k\) is the objective induced by a valid conic relaxation. If \(D_{k+1}\subseteq D_k\), \(\operatorname{diam}(D_k)\to0\), and \[0\le f(x)-\ell_k(x)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}(D_k))\quad\text{for every }x\in D_k,\] with \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\), then \[0\le p_k-L_k\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}(D_k))\to0.\] Thus spatial branching makes the conic lower bound asymptotically tight under uniform consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If relaxation error is uniformly controlled by a modulus of node diameter, nested domains with vanishing diameter have conic lower-bound gaps converging to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Shrinking Tightness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform error-modulus assumptions support the stated gap bound, and property fits the leaf. A source is needed for this domain-shrinking tightness regime and its connection to conic spatial relaxations.

children.title: Conic Oracle-Certificate Interface
children.top_down_role: Convex conic subproblem interfaces supplying lower bounds, cuts, feasibility information, and qualified statuses to global search.

assumptions_latex: The original feasible set restricted to node domain \(D\) is contained in a conic region \(R(D)\).
The oracle solves or validly bounds the conic relaxation.
The problem is a minimization problem with objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite oracle output \(L(D)\) satisfies \(L(D)\le\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap D\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-local lower-bound oracle with explicit validity contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node-domain conic oracle maps a branch-and-bound domain \(D\) to a status and, when finite, a value \[L(D):=\inf\{f(x):x\in R(D)\},\] where the conic relaxation satisfies \(F\cap D\subseteq R(D)\). Its validity contract is \[L(D)\le\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap D\}.\] A certified infeasibility status is admissible only when the relaxation \(R(D)\) is empty, which implies \(F\cap D=\varnothing\). The oracle may additionally return a dual solution or ray that independently certifies its bound or infeasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-domain conic oracle builds and solves a relaxation valid on one branch-and-bound domain, returning a certified lower bound or certified node infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Domain Conic Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound and infeasibility contracts are coherent, and definition is appropriate for the oracle leaf. No source supports the oracle semantics or returned certificate/status contract.

assumptions_latex: The mixed-integer variables are fixed at an assignment \(y=\bar y\).
The resulting continuous conic relaxation contains every feasible continuous completion of \(\bar y\).
The oracle solves or validly bounds that relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned value \(L(\bar y)\) lower-bounds the best feasible completion with integer assignment \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: continuous conic relaxation after fixing integers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle for the continuous subproblem induced by a fixed integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mixed-integer problem with integer vector \(y\), an integer-fixed conic oracle substitutes \(y=\bar y\) and constructs a continuous conic relaxation \(R(\bar y)\) containing every feasible continuous completion of that assignment. It returns \[L(\bar y):=\inf\{f(x,\bar y):x\in R(\bar y)\},\] which satisfies \[L(\bar y)\le\inf\{f(x,\bar y):(x,\bar y)\in F\}.\] If \(R(\bar y)=\varnothing\) is certified, then no feasible completion of \(\bar y\) exists; otherwise the bound applies only to that fixed assignment unless separately globalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing all integer variables, the oracle solves a continuous conic relaxation that bounds the best feasible completion or certifies that the assignment has none.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Fixed Conic Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-assignment validity and locality statements are mathematically coherent, and definition fits the leaf. A specifically located source is required for the completion-bound and infeasibility contract.

assumptions_latex: The node problem separates into blocks coupled only by \(\sum_i A_i x_i=b\).
Each block oracle returns a valid lower bound on its Lagrangian infimum.
The multiplier \(\lambda\) is shared consistently across all blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda\), \(L(\lambda):=\lambda^\top b+\sum_i q_i(\lambda)\) is a valid lower bound on the coupled node optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian aggregation of independently computed blockwise conic bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the node problem \(\inf\{\sum_i f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_i A_i x_i=b\}\). Given a multiplier \(\lambda\), block \(i\) computes a conic lower bound \[q_i(\lambda)\le\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)-\lambda^\top A_i x_i\bigr).\] The decomposed oracle aggregates the block outputs as \[L(\lambda):=\lambda^\top b+\sum_i q_i(\lambda).\] Weak duality gives \(L(\lambda)\le p^*\) for every \(\lambda\), where \(p^*\) is the coupled node optimum. The oracle may maximize \(L(\lambda)\) over admissible multipliers before returning its bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent conic block oracles bound Lagrangian subproblems; adding their bounds and the coupling term yields a valid lower bound for the coupled node problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed Conic Bound Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign convention and aggregated weak-duality bound are internally consistent, and algorithm fits the decomposed-oracle container. No source is cited for the decomposition procedure or multiplier optimization.

assumptions_latex: Oracle levels satisfy \(R_0(D)\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_m(D)\supseteq F\cap D\).
Each level returns a valid lower bound \(L_k(D)\).
Escalation terminates after finitely many levels or upon a declared resource limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned bound is valid and satisfies \(L_0(D)\le\cdots\le L_m(D)\le p(D)\) for every solved level.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive node oracle that increases conic strength while preserving lower-bound validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On node domain \(D\), initialize \(k:=0\). Solve the conic relaxation \(R_k(D)\) and obtain \(L_k(D):=\inf_{x\in R_k(D)}f(x)\). Return immediately if the node is pruned, the required bound accuracy is met, or the resource policy stops. Otherwise set \(k:=k+1\) and repeat with a stronger relaxation satisfying \(R_k(D)\subseteq R_{k-1}(D)\). For every solved level, \[L_0(D)\le L_1(D)\le\cdots\le L_k(D)\le p(D),\] where \(p(D):=\inf_{x\in F\cap D}f(x)\). The final returned finite value is therefore a valid node lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle begins with a cheap conic relaxation and escalates when needed. Nested feasible regions ensure every successive node lower bound is at least as strong.
knowledge_statements.title: Escalating-Strength Conic Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested relaxation sequence yields the stated monotone valid bounds, and algorithm is the correct role. The adaptive triggers, termination policy, and escalating-oracle architecture lack cited support.

assumptions_latex: For fixed master variables \(y\), the conic subproblem is \(Q(y)=\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b-By,\ x\in K\}\).
The cone \(K\) is closed and convex.
A dual-feasible pair \((\lambda,s)\) satisfies \(A^\top\lambda+s=c\) and \(s\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(\eta\ge(b-By)^\top\lambda\) is a globally valid lower-bound cut for every \(y\).

notation.meaning: master epigraph variable for the subproblem value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality-style master cut obtained from any dual-feasible conic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parameterized conic subproblem \[Q(y):=\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b-By,\ x\in K\},\] let \((\lambda,s)\) satisfy \(A^\top\lambda+s=c\) and \(s\in K^*\). Weak conic duality yields \[(b-By)^\top\lambda\le Q(y)\] for every parameter value \(y\) for which the primal subproblem is feasible. Hence a master variable \(\eta\) representing \(Q(y)\) may be constrained by the globally valid cut \[\eta\ge(b-By)^\top\lambda.\] Dual optimality and strong duality make the cut tight at the generating parameter, but are not required for its validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any dual-feasible conic solution defines an affine lower bound on the parameterized subproblem value, yielding a valid master epigraph cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Bound Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated dual convention, weak duality supports the affine bound cut without strong duality; certificate fits the cut container. A source with a specific theorem or section locator is required.

assumptions_latex: The conic feasibility system is \(Ax=b-By\), \(x\in K\), with closed convex cone \(K\).
A ray \(r\) satisfies \(A^\top r\in K^*\).
At the generating parameter \(\bar y\), \((b-B\bar y)^\top r<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \((b-By)^\top r\ge0\) is valid for every parameter admitting a conic-feasible completion and excludes \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility cut from a conic alternative-system ray; validity is separated from ray existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the parameterized conic system \[Ax=b-By,\qquad x\in K.\] If a vector \(r\) satisfies \(A^\top r\in K^*\), then every feasible pair \((x,y)\) obeys \[(b-By)^\top r=x^\top A^\top r\ge0.\] Therefore the inequality \[(b-By)^\top r\ge0\] is a valid feasibility cut in the parameter space. If the generating parameter \(\bar y\) satisfies \((b-B\bar y)^\top r<0\), the ray certifies infeasibility of its conic subproblem and the cut excludes \(\bar y\). Additional regularity may be required to guarantee that every infeasible conic system admits such a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual ray nonnegative on the cone yields a parameter-space feasibility cut. A negative evaluation at the generating assignment certifies its infeasibility and excludes it.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ray Feasibility Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ray condition makes the feasibility cut valid and a negative evaluation excludes the generating parameter; certificate fits the leaf. A specifically located source is required, especially for conditions governing ray existence.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregated Certificate Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single master-space cut obtained by summing blockwise conic certificate inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\prod_{i=1}^q K_i\) and consider \(A_i x+B_i z-b_i\in K_i\) for every \(i\). If \(y_i\in K_i^*\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^q A_i^{\mathsf T}y_i=0\), then every feasible \(z\) satisfies the aggregated certificate cut
\[
\sum_{i=1}^q\langle y_i,B_i z-b_i\rangle\ge 0.
\]
At a tested point \(\bar z\), strict negativity of the left-hand side excludes \(\bar z\). The aggregation is valid even when the individual terms are not separately valid cuts, because cancellation of the continuous-variable coefficients is required only after summation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block dual certificates combine into one valid master cut when their continuous-variable coefficients cancel in aggregate.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone for each \(i\).
\(y_i\in K_i^*\) for each \(i\).
\(\sum_i A_i^{\mathsf T}y_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^q\langle y_i,B_i z-b_i\rangle\ge 0\) for every feasible \(z\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of block cone K_i
dual certificate component for block i

review_flags: Exact conic certificate-cut formulation needs a directly supporting MICP source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregation claim is mathematically plausible and fits the representation leaf, but no supporting citation is supplied and the domains and dimensions of x, A_i, B_i, and b_i are not introduced. A direct conic-MICP decomposition source is needed to confirm the intended formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Certificate Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate certificate cuts retained when each component independently eliminates continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For conic blocks \(A_i x+B_i z-b_i\in K_i\), suppose certificate vectors \(y_i\in K_i^*\) satisfy \(A_i^{\mathsf T}y_i=0\) individually. Then every feasible master point satisfies the disaggregated family
\[
\langle y_i,B_i z-b_i\rangle\ge 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,q.
\]
Keeping these inequalities separately is at least as strong as retaining only their sum. If only \(\sum_i A_i^{\mathsf T}y_i=0\) holds, the separate inequalities are not generally valid; only the aggregated cut is justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate may be split into separate cuts only when every component independently removes the continuous variables.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone for each \(i\).
\(A_i^{\mathsf T}y_i=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y_i,B_i z-b_i\rangle\ge0\) for every feasible \(z\) and every \(i\).
review_flags: Disaggregation convention varies across conic decomposition methods; a direct source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The individual annihilation conditions do justify separate block cuts and the representation kind fits, but no source supports this particular disaggregation convention. The spaces and dimensions of x, z, A_i, B_i, and b_i are also unspecified.

children.title: Global Certificate Cuts
children.top_down_role: Certificate-derived cuts valid across the global feasible domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Certificate Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate cuts valid throughout the original master domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be the original master domain and let \(F\subseteq Z\) be exactly the set of master points extendable to feasible continuous variables. An inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\) is a global certificate cut if \[F\subseteq\{z\in Z:\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\}.\] Its validity does not depend on assumptions specific to the node at which its certificate was generated. Consequently, it may be imposed at the root and inherited by every search node whose domain is contained in \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global certificate cut is valid for every globally feasible master projection without relying on node-specific assumptions, so it may be inherited throughout the search tree.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is the original master domain.
\(F\) is exactly the projection of the global feasible set onto the master variables.
The cut derivation uses no node-specific assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq\{z\in Z:\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\}\).

notation.meaning: projection of the global feasible set onto the master variables

review_flags: A direct source is required for the certificate-cut specialization and search-tree inheritance terminology.

children.title: Node-Local Certificate Cuts
children.top_down_role: Certificate-derived cuts valid only within a specified search-node domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Local Certificate Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate cuts whose validity depends on restrictions active at one search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search node \(N\), let \(Z_N\subseteq Z\) be its master domain and \(F_N=F\cap Z_N\). An inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\) is node-local when \(F_N\subseteq\{z:\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\}\), but global validity over \(F\) has not been established. Its validity may use bounds, branching decisions, local relaxations, or domain-dependent reformulations active at \(N\). It may be inherited only by descendants whose domains preserve every assumption used in its derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-local cut is certified only on a node domain and on descendants retaining all derivation assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_N\subseteq Z\) is the domain defined by node assumptions.
The certificate derivation is valid throughout \(Z_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_N\subseteq\{z:\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\ge\beta\}\), without implying validity on \(F\setminus F_N\).

notation.meaning: globally feasible master projections lying in Z_N

review_flags: A direct source is needed for the locality convention used by this taxonomy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and its content kind fits the locality-taxonomy leaf, but no cited source establishes the proposed certificate-cut locality and descendant-inheritance convention.

children.title: Locality Qualification
children.top_down_role: Structural information used to classify the domain of validity for a certificate cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Locality Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical test determining a domain on which a certificate derivation establishes cut validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be the master domain, let \(F\subseteq Z\) be the feasible master projection, and let \(c:Z\to\mathbb R\) define a candidate cut \(c(z)\ge0\). Let \(H\) collect all assumptions used in its derivation and let \(D(H)\subseteq Z\) be the set on which those assumptions hold. Suppose the derivation establishes \[z\in F\cap D(H)\Longrightarrow c(z)\ge0.\] A proposed validity domain \(D\subseteq Z\) is assumption-qualified when \(F\cap D\subseteq D(H)\). Under this qualification, \(c(z)\ge0\) is valid for every \(z\in F\cap D\). The derivation is globally qualified when \(F\subseteq D(H)\), and it is qualified at a node with domain \(Z_N\) when \(F\cap Z_N\subseteq D(H)\). Numerical validity at only the generating point does not establish either qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate derivation qualifies a cut on a proposed domain when every feasible point in that domain satisfies all assumptions used by the derivation.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is the master domain and \(F\subseteq Z\) is its feasible projection.
\(D(H)\) is the set on which every premise in \(H\) holds.
\(z\in F\cap D(H)\) implies \(c(z)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F\cap D\subseteq D(H)\), then \(c(z)\ge0\) for every \(z\in F\cap D\).

notation.meaning: all assumptions used by the certificate derivation
domain on which all derivation assumptions hold

review_flags: The corrected logical qualification still requires a source matching the intended algorithmic locality convention.

children.title: Cut Inheritance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring locally valid certificate cuts through the search tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Inheritance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact search-tree boundary beyond which a local certificate cut cannot be propagated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a cut \(c(z)\ge0\) is qualified on \(D(H)\), and node \(N\) satisfies \(Z_N\subseteq D(H)\). A descendant \(M\) may inherit the cut whenever \(Z_M\subseteq D(H)\). Propagation must stop at any node \(L\) for which \(F\cap Z_L\nsubseteq D(H)\), unless the cut is independently requalified there. Thus ancestry alone is insufficient: inheritance is controlled by preservation of the certificate's assumptions. A globally qualified cut has no such search-tree boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local cut passes only to nodes whose feasible domains retain every assumption used to certify it.
assumptions_latex: The cut is valid on \(D(H)\).
Node domains represent all active branching and bound restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inheritance to \(M\) is valid if \(F\cap Z_M\subseteq D(H)\), and is unjustified otherwise.
review_flags: Search-tree inheritance rule needs confirmation from a source treating local conic cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inheritance rule is logically reasonable when interpreted relative to the stated certificate derivation, and property is an appropriate content kind. No source is supplied for local conic-cut propagation or requalification boundaries.

children.title: Conic Infeasibility Certificate for MICP
children.top_down_role: Continuous conic alternatives used for pruning, with explicit separation from integrality infeasibility and pathological noncertification.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Outer Approximation With Conic Certificates for Mixed-Integer Convex Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Infeasible conic subproblems and feasibility cuts
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Outer Approximation With Conic Certificates for Mixed-Integer Convex Problems

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Conic Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict-separation certificate for an infeasible conic continuous subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the conic system \(Ax+c\in K\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. A strong infeasibility certificate is a vector \(y\in K^*\) satisfying
\[
 A^{\mathsf T}y=0,
 \qquad
 \langle y,c\rangle<0.
\]
Indeed, every feasible \(x\) would give \(\langle y,Ax+c\rangle=\langle y,c\rangle\ge0\), contradicting strict negativity. Moreover, the certificate supplies the positive separation margin \(-\langle y,c\rangle/\lVert y\rVert\) when \(y\ne0\), thereby certifying strong rather than merely weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-cone vector annihilating the linear image and strictly separating the offset certifies strong conic infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\).
\(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(\langle y,c\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(Ax+c\in K\) is strongly infeasible.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the linear map A

review_flags: Standard conic alternative result, but no conic-analysis source or exact theorem locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict dual-separation conditions are standard and certificate is the correct content kind, but no authoritative conic-analysis theorem locator is supplied. The domain and codomain of A and the ambient space of x and c should also be fixed by that source.

children.title: Weakly Infeasible Conic Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Conic subproblem regimes exhibiting weak infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Infeasible Conic Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasible conic systems having zero distance from the target cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite-dimensional conic system \(Ax+c\in K\) is weakly infeasible when it has no feasible point but
\[
\inf_{x}\operatorname{dist}(Ax+c,K)=0.
\]
Equivalently, there exists a sequence \((x_k)\) with \(Ax_k+c\notin K\) for every \(k\), while \(\operatorname{dist}(Ax_k+c,K)\to0\). Weak infeasibility excludes any strict-separation certificate \(y\in K^*\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(\langle y,c\rangle<0\), because such a vector would impose a positive distance from \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly infeasible conic system is infeasible but can approach the cone arbitrarily closely and has no strict separator.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in finite dimensions.
The system \(Ax+c\in K\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak infeasibility holds exactly when \(\inf_x\operatorname{dist}(Ax+c,K)=0\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from u to K

review_flags: The definition is standard, but the inventory provides no conic weak-infeasibility source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-distance characterization is the standard finite-dimensional notion of weak infeasibility and the definition kind fits. No conic-duality source is cited, and the domain of x and linear map A is not explicitly introduced.

children.title: Certificate Nonexistence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where standard finite conic certificates are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Nonexistence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regimes where ordinary strict conic alternative certificates cannot exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax+c\in K\), an ordinary strong certificate requires \(y\in K^*\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(\langle y,c\rangle<0\). No such vector exists when the system is weakly infeasible. More generally, nonexistence occurs whenever the disjoint convex sets \(c+\operatorname{range}(A)\) and \(K\) have zero distance and hence admit no strict separator of this form. Consequently, failure to obtain a strong certificate does not certify feasibility; it may reflect weak infeasibility or a nonclosed projection or linear-image geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-distance infeasibility can prevent strict dual certificates, so absence of a certificate cannot be interpreted as feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimensions.
\((c+\operatorname{range}(A))\cap K=\varnothing\).
\(\operatorname{dist}(c+\operatorname{range}(A),K)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(y\in K^*\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(\langle y,c\rangle<0\).
review_flags: A conic duality source is required for the precise certificate-nonexistence boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-distance regime precludes the stated strict separator, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A conic separation or alternatives theorem with an exact locator is required to support the claimed boundary and the reference to nonclosed image geometry.

children.title: Indeterminate Oracle Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Oracle outcomes that do not establish feasibility, infeasibility, or a qualified bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Oracle Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle status when neither feasibility nor a valid infeasibility certificate is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic oracle outcome is indeterminate if it returns neither a primal point satisfying the declared feasibility tolerance nor a verifiable dual certificate proving infeasibility or a valid bound. This includes iteration-limit, numerical-failure, unknown-status, and suspected weak-infeasibility outcomes. Formally, if the returned data establish neither \(r_{\mathrm p}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}\) nor all predicates defining a certificate \(y\), then no logical conclusion about feasibility follows. In particular, the global algorithm may not convert an indeterminate status into an infeasibility cut or fathom the associated node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a verified primal solution or certificate, an oracle status is indeterminate and cannot justify a cut or node pruning.
assumptions_latex: The oracle uses declared primal and certificate verification tolerances.
Neither the primal acceptance predicate nor the certificate predicate is verified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outcome proves neither feasibility nor infeasibility and cannot alone justify node fathoming.
review_flags: Safe interpretation of solver statuses needs a source specifying conic-oracle verification semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The safety interpretation is plausible and failure_boundary fits, but the predicates for a verifiable certificate or bound are not specified and no solver-oracle source defines the listed statuses or their permitted algorithmic interpretation.

children.title: Safe Node-Disposition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on pruning or retaining nodes when conic certification is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Safe Node-Disposition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal certification requirements for pruning or retaining an MICP search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node may be fathomed for conic infeasibility only when a verified certificate proves infeasibility throughout its node domain. It may be fathomed by bound only when a certified valid lower bound is no better than the incumbent under the stated optimality tolerance. If the conic oracle is indeterminate, suspected weakly infeasible, or supplies only an unverified numerical ray, neither disposition is justified. The safe action is to retain the node, strengthen or reformulate the subproblem, invoke a more reliable oracle, or defer the node without claiming a proof of exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune only with a domain-valid infeasibility certificate or certified bound; otherwise retain or defer the node.
assumptions_latex: Node pruning must preserve completeness of the global search.
All certificates and bounds are independently checked on their claimed domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An uncertified or indeterminate oracle outcome is insufficient for node fathoming.

notation.meaning: certified lower bound at node N

review_flags: Algorithmic safety rule needs a directly supporting global MICP reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly separates certified pruning from indeterminate outcomes, but the bound-fathoming inequality and minimization convention are not stated explicitly. A global MICP source is needed for both the certification rule and safe disposition behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Domain Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate proving absence of feasible extensions throughout a restricted search-node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a node impose \(z\in Z_N\), and consider \(Ax+Bz-b\in K\). A node-domain infeasibility certificate is data defining a function \(y:Z_N\to K^*\) such that, for every \(z\in Z_N\),
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y(z)=0,
\qquad
\langle y(z),Bz-b\rangle<0.
\]
These inequalities contradict conic feasibility for every master point in \(Z_N\); hence the node contains no feasible mixed-integer conic solution. A certificate computed only at one \(\bar z\in Z_N\) excludes that point but does not certify the entire node unless its validity extends over all of \(Z_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node certificate must establish conic infeasibility for every master point in the node domain, not merely one trial point.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_N\) contains every master point permitted at node \(N\).
\(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The displayed certificate conditions hold for every \(z\in Z_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \((x,z)\) with \(z\in Z_N\) and \(Ax+Bz-b\in K\).
review_flags: The quantified node-domain certificate is mathematically sound but needs a source matching the intended MICP implementation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise family y(z) logically proves infeasibility throughout the node domain and certificate is the correct kind. No source establishes that this infinitely indexed object is the intended node-domain certificate in the MICP interface or explains how it is finitely represented and verified.

assumptions_latex: The node relaxation separates integrality from a continuous conic feasibility system.
A conic oracle certifies only infeasibility of the continuous system presented to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuous conic infeasibility certificates do not, by themselves, certify infeasibility caused solely by integrality.

notation.meaning: continuous relaxation feasible set at the current node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between continuous conic infeasibility and infeasibility caused only by integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set of the continuous conic relaxation at a search node, and require \(x_i\in\mathbb{Z}\) for every \(i\in I\). A conic infeasibility certificate for \(R\) proves mixed-integer infeasibility when it establishes \(R=\varnothing\). If \(R\neq\varnothing\) but \(R\cap\{x:x_i\in\mathbb{Z},\ i\in I\}=\varnothing\), no certificate asserting only continuous conic infeasibility exists. For example, \(R=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:x=1/2\}\) is continuously feasible, whereas \(R\cap\mathbb{Z}=\varnothing\). Thus integrality-only infeasibility requires discrete reasoning, such as branching, enumeration, or an integer-valid contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic certificate proves mixed-integer infeasibility when the continuous relaxation is empty, but cannot alone detect a feasible relaxation containing no integer point.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Infeasibility Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is mathematically coherent and matches the terminal context, but no inspectable citation supports the conic-versus-integrality distinction or the stated recovery methods.

children.title: Conic Outer-Approximation Masters
children.top_down_role: Master-relaxation forms retaining certificate-derived approximations.

assumptions_latex: Every stored inequality is valid for the node relaxation being approximated.
The master retains the original discrete restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting mixed-integer polyhedron is an outer approximation and yields a valid lower bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral outer-approximation master generated from valid oracle certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible region \(F\subseteq X\), where \(X\) includes the required integrality restrictions, let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite collection of certificate-derived inequalities \(a_c^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_c\) valid for every \(x\in F\). The polyhedral certificate master has feasible region \[P_{\mathcal C}=X\cap\bigcap_{c\in\mathcal C}\{x:a_c^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_c\}.\] Hence \(F\subseteq P_{\mathcal C}\). Minimizing the master objective over \(P_{\mathcal C}\) gives a lower bound on the minimum over \(F\). Adding another globally valid certificate inequality can only contract \(P_{\mathcal C}\) and cannot invalidate that bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral certificate master intersects integrality restrictions with finitely many valid certificate cuts, producing an outer approximation and a valid minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Certificate Masters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and lower-bound claim fit a polyhedral certificate master, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator supporting this formulation.

assumptions_latex: Retained conic constraints and added linear cuts are valid for the original feasible region.
The master preserves all required integrality restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed master remains an outer approximation and its minimization value is a valid lower bound.

notation.meaning: finite pool of valid linear cuts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-approximation master retaining selected conic structure alongside certificate cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the original mixed-integer feasible region and let \(X\) encode its variable domains and integrality restrictions. Suppose \(Gx-g\in K\) is valid for all \(x\in F\), and every cut \(a_c^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_c\), with \(c\in\mathcal C\), is also valid on \(F\). A mixed conic-polyhedral master is represented by \[M_{\mathcal C}=\{x\in X:Gx-g\in K,\ a_c^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_c\ \text{for all }c\in\mathcal C\}.\] Then \(F\subseteq M_{\mathcal C}\). Consequently, for minimization, the optimum over \(M_{\mathcal C}\) is a valid lower bound, while additional valid cuts monotonically strengthen the master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed master retains selected conic constraints and combines them with valid linear cuts while preserving a valid outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Conic–Polyhedral Masters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed conic–polyhedral representation is internally consistent and appropriately classified, but it has no cited evidence with an inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: The lifted formulation projects onto a superset of the original feasible region.
All variable-domain and integrality restrictions required by the master are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization over the lifted master gives a valid bound, and projection recovers its formulation in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted outer-approximation master whose projection controls validity in original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\) be the original feasible region. An extended-formulation master introduces auxiliary variables \(w\in W\) and a tractable set \(Q\subseteq X\times W\) satisfying \[F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in X:\exists w\in W,\ (x,w)\in Q\}.\] Certificate inequalities may be imposed in the lifted space provided they are valid for every lifted representative used for points of \(F\). For an objective depending only on \(x\), minimizing over \(Q\) is equivalent to minimizing over \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\) and gives a valid lower bound on minimization over \(F\). Exact projection equality yields an exact extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended master uses auxiliary variables; its projection must contain the original feasible region so that optimization supplies a valid bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Formulation Masters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection-based representation and bound claim match extended-formulation masters, but no source is cited for the stated formulation and certificate-validity condition.

children.title: Global Cut Pools
children.top_down_role: Storage and reuse of cuts qualified for global validity.

assumptions_latex: Each admitted cut is valid for the original unspecialized feasible region.
Validity does not depend on temporary node bounds or local branching assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cut in the pool may be enforced at every search node without excluding a globally feasible point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally reusable cuts independent of branch-and-bound node assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the original feasible region. A global cut pool \(\mathcal G\) is a collection of inequalities \(g_j(x)\leq0\) such that \[g_j(x)\leq0\quad\text{for every }x\in F\text{ and every }j\in\mathcal G.\] Membership in \(\mathcal G\) requires validity without using node-specific bounds, branching decisions, or other temporary restrictions. Therefore each inequality in \(\mathcal G\) remains valid on \(F\cap D_v\) for every search-node domain \(D_v\), and it may be copied to any node master without changing the set of globally feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global cut pool contains inequalities valid for the original feasible region independently of node-specific assumptions, so every node may reuse them.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Cut Pools

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition captures globally valid, node-independent cuts and fits the locality hierarchy, but it lacks an inspectable source citation.

children.title: Node-Local Cut Pools
children.top_down_role: Storage of cuts tied to particular node domains or subtrees.

assumptions_latex: A search node has domain \(D_v\).
Each stored cut is valid on the node-restricted feasible region but need not be globally valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A node-local cut may be enforced only where its validity assumptions remain implied by the active node domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cuts whose validity depends on the domain or assumptions of a search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search node \(v\) with domain \(D_v\), a node-local cut pool \(\mathcal L_v\) is a collection of inequalities \(\ell_j(x)\leq0\) satisfying \[\ell_j(x)\leq0\quad\text{for every }x\in F\cap D_v\text{ and every }j\in\mathcal L_v.\] Such an inequality need not be valid on all of \(F\). It may therefore be enforced at node \(v\) and at a descendant \(w\) whenever \(D_w\subseteq D_v\). Transfer to an unrelated node or ancestor requires a separate validity check; otherwise the cut can exclude a feasible point and invalidate bounds or infeasibility conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-local pool contains cuts valid under one node's domain assumptions; descendants may inherit them, but unrelated nodes require revalidation.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Local Cut Pools

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes node-local validity and descendant inheritance, but no cited source supports the locality and transfer claims.

children.title: Cut-Pool Transfer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Validity-sensitive movement of cuts between local and global storage scopes.

assumptions_latex: Each cut records a validity domain.
The receiving node has a known active domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer is sound exactly when the receiving feasible region is contained in the cut's validity region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient validity test for transferring a cut between node pools.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a cut \(c(x)\leq0\) have validity region \(V_c\), meaning that \(c(x)\leq0\) holds for every \(x\in F\cap V_c\). Transfer of this cut to a receiving node \(w\) is sound precisely when \[F\cap D_w\subseteq V_c,\] or when an independently verified argument establishes \(c(x)\leq0\) throughout \(F\cap D_w\). Global transfer corresponds to \(F\subseteq V_c\). Descendant transfer is automatically valid when \(V_c=D_v\) for an originating node \(v\) and \(D_w\subseteq D_v\). If containment is unknown, the cut must remain quarantined from the receiving master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut can move to another node exactly when the receiver's feasible region lies inside the cut's recorded validity region, or validity is independently re-established.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Pool Transfer Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer condition is mathematically coherent when the recorded validity region is interpreted as a certified region, but no inspectable source supports the proposed regime.

children.title: Cut Locality Metadata
children.top_down_role: Provenance and domain metadata supporting safe cut-pool reuse.

assumptions_latex: Each generated cut has identifiable derivation assumptions and a validity region.
Metadata is retained with the cut throughout storage and transfer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metadata determines where the cut may be activated and what must be rechecked before transfer.

notation.meaning: domain on which the inequality is certified valid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical validity data attached to a cut for reliable activation and transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cut locality metadata for an inequality \(c(x)\leq0\) is a record containing at least its certified validity region \(V_c\), its derivation assumptions \(A_c\), and its locality class. The record asserts \[A_c\Longrightarrow c(x)\leq0\quad\text{for every }x\in F\cap V_c.\] The locality class is global when \(F\subseteq V_c\) without node assumptions, and node-local when validity depends on a specified node domain. Activating or transferring the cut is permitted only when the current model implies \(A_c\) and its feasible region is contained in \(V_c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut locality metadata records the certified validity region, derivation assumptions, and locality class needed to decide sound activation or transfer.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Locality Metadata

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metadata definition fits the terminal container, but its required fields and activation rule are uncited design claims rather than source-supported candidate knowledge.

assumptions_latex: An oracle-generated certificate is used to derive a cut, bound, or infeasibility decision.
The derivation inputs can be identified and retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A provenance record makes the certificate's applicability and downstream uses auditable and reproducible.

notation.meaning: model and node data supplied to the oracle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Audit record connecting an oracle certificate to assumptions, validation, and derived artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificate provenance for an oracle output \(y\) is an immutable record linking \(y\) to the submitted data \(D\), the node domain, oracle status, numerical tolerances, validation results, and every derived artifact \(q\). It records a checkable implication of the form \[D\ \text{and validated }y\Longrightarrow q\text{ is valid on }V,\] where \(V\) is the declared validity region. Any transformation, strengthening, or transfer creates a new linked record rather than replacing the original. A cut, bound, or pruning decision may rely on \(q\) only while its active assumptions and domain satisfy the recorded implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provenance tracking links each certificate to its oracle input, node, tolerances, validation, validity region, and every cut or decision derived from it.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Provenance Tracking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The provenance definition matches the reliability-system context, but the asserted immutable schema, transformation policy, and reliance rule have no cited source.

children.title: Ambiguous Oracle Statuses
children.top_down_role: Solver statuses lacking a unique certified interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The oracle returns neither a qualified feasible conclusion nor a qualified infeasibility certificate.
The global algorithm requires certified bounds or exclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An ambiguous status cannot justify pruning, a global cut, or an incumbent update without additional validation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary for oracle responses that establish no certified mathematical conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a node relaxation \(R_v\), call an oracle status \(s\) ambiguous when it supplies neither a point satisfying the prescribed feasibility checks nor a certificate satisfying the prescribed infeasibility or bound checks. Examples include unknown, interrupted, numerical failure, and unresolved infeasible-or-unbounded responses. From such an \(s\), neither \(R_v=\varnothing\) nor \(R_v\neq\varnothing\) follows. Consequently, \(s\) alone cannot support node pruning, a globally valid cut, a certified bound, or acceptance of an incumbent. The algorithm must preserve the node or invoke a recovery procedure that produces a separately qualified conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambiguous oracle response proves neither feasibility nor infeasibility and therefore cannot alone justify pruning, global cuts, certified bounds, or incumbent acceptance.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous Oracle Statuses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is logically consistent and appropriately classified, but the examples and prohibited downstream uses require an authoritative oracle-status or solver source.

children.title: Inaccurate Oracle Statuses
children.top_down_role: Statuses affected by numerical error or inadequate solution accuracy.

assumptions_latex: The oracle labels a result as numerically inaccurate or returns residuals outside certified tolerances.
The result would otherwise affect a globally consequential decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The status label alone is insufficient; only independently qualified mathematical evidence may be used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Use boundary for approximate oracle conclusions that fail prescribed certification tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inaccurate oracle status reports a candidate \(x\) or certificate \(y\) for which the oracle does not guarantee the prescribed residual, cone-membership, integrality, or duality conditions within tolerance \(\tau\). Such a status is not itself a proof of feasibility, infeasibility, or a valid objective bound. A downstream decision is permitted only if independent checks establish the exact implication required by that decision, or establish a rigorously tolerance-aware substitute. Otherwise the result must not prune a node, update a certified incumbent, or generate a globally reusable cut; it remains provisional and triggers recovery or re-solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inaccurate status is not a certificate. Its candidate may be used only after independent checks establish the conditions needed by the intended decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Inaccurate Oracle Statuses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary classification and validation principle fit the terminal context, but no source supports the interpretation and permitted uses of inaccurate statuses.

children.title: Status Qualification Checks
children.top_down_role: Evidence used to determine whether an oracle status is suitable for global search.

knowledge_statements.title: Status Qualification Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Action-specific validation of oracle outputs before they influence the global search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A status qualification check evaluates an oracle output \(z\) against the submitted model \(D_v\) and tolerances \(\tau\). For a primal claim it checks variable domains, integrality when required, constraint residuals, and objective consistency. For a bound or infeasibility claim it checks certificate dimensions, sign and cone membership, the defining certificate identities or inequalities, and compatibility with the node domain. The status is qualified for an action \(a\) only when these checks establish the mathematical implication required by \(a\). Qualification for one action does not imply qualification for another; any failed or unavailable required check leaves the output uncertified for that action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification checks validate residuals, domains, cone membership, certificate identities, and objective data specifically for each proposed global-search action.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns a candidate primal point, bound, or infeasibility certificate.
Acceptance tolerances and the submitted model data are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing all checks relevant to the intended action qualifies the status for that action; failure leaves it uncertified.

children.title: Conservative Recovery Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Safe fallback limits when an oracle status cannot be qualified.

knowledge_statements.title: Conservative Recovery Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary governing safe use of uncertified conic-oracle responses in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node with feasible region \(X_N\) and incumbent value \(U\), let an oracle return status \(s\), candidate value \(v\), and certificate \(c\). If \(c\) does not verify either \(v\leq \inf_{x\in X_N} f(x)\) or \(X_N=\varnothing\), then neither pruning nor globally valid cut generation may rely on \((s,v)\). Conservative recovery may only retain previously verified bounds and cuts, replace the node bound by \(-\infty\), and re-solve or branch. Thus an uncertified response cannot remove any point of \(X_N\) or increase the certified global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a verifiable bound or infeasibility certificate, the solver must preserve the node, discard the claimed bound, and recover by re-solving or branching.
assumptions_latex: \(\min\{f(x):x\in X_N\}\) is the node problem.
\(U\) is obtained from a verified feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncertified oracle information cannot justify pruning, globally valid cuts, or a larger certified lower bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and conservative principle fit the leaf, but no source supports the exact reset, pruning, and cut-use policy. The wording also should clarify whether a previously certified node bound is retained or replaced by negative infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Certificate Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fail-safe recovery procedure for an oracle response lacking a required certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given node \(N\), incumbent \(U\), stored verified lower bound \(L_N^{\mathrm{old}}\), and an oracle response without a verifiable certificate, initialize the recovered node with \(L_N:=L_N^{\mathrm{old}}\) and retain only previously validated cuts. Query a qualified oracle again using tighter tolerances or an alternative formulation. If a valid lower-bound or infeasibility certificate is obtained, update or prune \(N\) accordingly; otherwise partition \(N\) into children whose union covers its feasible region. Stop when certification succeeds or the node is replaced by covering children; never prune solely because certification remains unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retry with a qualified oracle; if certification still fails, keep the old valid bound and branch into children covering the unresolved node.
assumptions_latex: The search is a minimization algorithm.
Child feasible regions cover the parent feasible region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovery step preserves every feasible point not already excluded by verified information.

notation.meaning: previously certified lower bound for node N

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, and the fail-safe coverage principle is plausible, but the prescribed retry-and-branch recovery policy has no cited source and is architecture dependent.

children.title: Spatial Branch-Cut Search for Nonconvex MICP
children.top_down_role: Global search coordinating discrete branching, spatial partitioning, conic bounds, separation, reduction, fathoming, and incumbent discovery.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Branching; convergence and finiteness; domain reduction; fathoming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Branching and Bounds Tightening Techniques for Non-convex MINLP
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Spatial branch-and-bound; bound tightening; reliability branching

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Relaxation; separation; propagation; branching; primal heuristics
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Global Optimization of Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programs with SCIP 8.0

knowledge_statements.title: Unified Discrete–Spatial Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-tree branch-and-bound over integer decisions and continuous nonconvex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{f(x,z):(x,z)\in F,\ z\in\mathbb Z^p\}\), initialize one root region \(R_0=X\times Z\), incumbent \(U=+\infty\), and an active-node list. At node \(R\), solve a valid relaxation to obtain \(L(R)\). Prune if infeasibility is certified or \(L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\); update \(U\) using verified feasible points. Otherwise branch either on a fractional integer component or by spatially partitioning a continuous interval, producing children whose feasible portions cover that of \(R\). Stop when no active node has lower bound below \(U-\varepsilon\), and return the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One branch-and-bound tree interleaves integer branching and continuous spatial partitioning while using valid relaxations to prune nodes.
assumptions_latex: The initial variable domains are bounded.
Every node relaxation supplies a valid lower bound.
Branching children cover the parent feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon termination, the returned incumbent is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176
3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176
