knowledge_statements.title: Finite Certificate-Generation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-certificate criterion for exact termination of deterministic global MICP methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a minimization problem, with finite optimum \(v^*\) when feasible, and let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite certificate family. Suppose every nonterminal iteration consumes a distinct previously unused certificate \(c\in\mathcal C\), certificates are never regenerated, and exhaustion of the applicable certificates establishes either infeasibility or a valid global lower bound equal to the value \(U\) of a feasible incumbent. With exact oracle computations, the procedure terminates after at most \(|\mathcal C|\) certificate-consuming iterations and returns either an infeasibility certificate or a globally optimal incumbent satisfying \(U=v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite exact termination follows when every nonterminal iteration permanently consumes a new member of a finite exhaustive certificate family, whose exhaustion proves infeasibility or closes the global optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(|\mathcal C|<\infty\), and consumed certificates are never regenerated.
Every nonterminal iteration consumes a distinct unused certificate.
Certificate exhaustion proves infeasibility or produces a valid global lower bound equal to a feasible incumbent value.
All certificate, incumbent, and bounding computations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure has at most \(|\mathcal C|\) certificate-consuming iterations and terminates with infeasibility or \(U=v^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Zero-Tolerance Finiteness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for finite termination with an exact, zero optimality-gap stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a global minimization algorithm with valid bounds \(L_t\le v^*\le U_t\) and zero-tolerance stopping rule \(U_t-L_t=0\). Exact finite termination is guaranteed if there exists \(T<\infty\) such that the algorithm produces \(L_T=U_T\), for example because it exhausts a finite search partition using exact arithmetic and exact subproblem oracles. Mere convergence \(L_t\uparrow v^*\) and \(U_t\downarrow v^*\) is insufficient: the positive gap may satisfy \(U_t-L_t>0\) for every finite \(t\). Hence zero-tolerance finiteness requires finite attainment of bound equality, not only asymptotic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-gap rule terminates finitely only when exact bound equality is attained at a finite iteration; asymptotic convergence alone does not suffice.
assumptions_latex: \(L_t\le v^*\le U_t\) for every iteration \(t\).
Termination is declared exactly when \(U_t-L_t=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite termination requires finite attainment: \(\exists T<\infty\) such that \(L_T=U_T=v^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Nonconvex Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case hardness inherited from the binary linear subclass of nonconvex MICP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decision version of global mixed-integer nonconvex optimization is NP-hard. Indeed, its problem class contains binary linear feasibility: given rational \(A\), \(b\), decide whether there exists \(z\in\{0,1\}^p\) satisfying \(Az\le b\). This subclass already represents NP-complete problems such as 0–1 integer programming. Consequently, any algorithm solving every rational nonconvex MICP globally in time polynomial in the binary input length would solve every instance of that subclass in polynomial time. Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no such general polynomial-time global algorithm exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General nonconvex MICP is NP-hard because it contains binary linear feasibility, so a universal polynomial-time global solver would imply P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: All numerical data are rational and represented in binary.
The problem class permits binary variables and linear constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General rational nonconvex MICP is NP-hard; polynomial-time global solution of all instances would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Quadratic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness of binary quadratic maximization through the weighted maximum-cut formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative integer weights \(w_{ij}\), and threshold \(K\), consider whether
\[\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\ge K.\]
The objective equals the weight of the cut encoded by \(x\). The decision problem is therefore weighted MAX-CUT and is NP-complete; membership in NP follows by evaluating a proposed binary vector. Hence globally maximizing a quadratic function over a binary box is NP-hard, even though the displayed quadratic is convex and the nonconvexity arises from maximizing it and imposing integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary quadratic maximization is NP-hard: the sum of weighted squared endpoint differences exactly represents a weighted graph cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) and all \(w_{ij},K\) are encoded in binary.
\(w_{ij}\ge0\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deciding whether the displayed quadratic maximum is at least \(K\) is NP-complete.

notation.meaning: binary indicator assigning vertex i to one side of a cut

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Factor Approximation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation criterion for nonnegative minimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be a minimization instance of binary length \(n\), with feasible set \(F(I)\), nonnegative objective \(f_I\), and optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). A polynomial-factor approximation regime exists on an instance class \(\mathcal I\) if an algorithm runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and returns \(x\in F(I)\) satisfying
\[f_I(x)\le \rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\]
for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), where \(1\le\rho(n)\le n^c\) for some constant \(c\). If zero optima are allowed, the convention must separately require exact zero recognition or use an additive guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-factor approximation runs in polynomial time and returns a feasible value within a factor bounded by a polynomial in input length.
assumptions_latex: \(f_I(x)\ge0\) for every feasible \(x\).
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\) under the multiplicative convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The guarantee is \(f_I(x)\le\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) with \(\rho(n)\le n^c\).

children.title: Approximation-Scheme Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Scheme Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS and FPTAS regimes for nonnegative minimization over restricted MICP classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a class \(\mathcal I\) of minimization instances with positive optimum, a polynomial-time approximation scheme is a family of algorithms \(\{A_\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon<1\}\) such that \(A_\varepsilon(I)\) returns a feasible \(x\) with
\[f_I(x)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I),\]
and, for each fixed \(\varepsilon\), runs in time polynomial in the input length \(n\). It is a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme when its running time is polynomial jointly in \(n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\). The definition applies only to the stated instance class and objective normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PTAS achieves any fixed relative accuracy in polynomial input time; an FPTAS is also polynomial in the reciprocal accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
The objective is nonnegative and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A PTAS guarantees \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation; an FPTAS additionally has runtime polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\).

children.title: Inapproximability Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Hardness frontiers limiting achievable approximation quality under stated complexity premises.

knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity-theoretic boundaries on multiplicative approximation factors for a specified problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a class of minimization instances with nonnegative objectives and positive optimum, and let \(H\) be an explicit complexity assumption. A factor \(r(n)\ge 1\) is an inapproximability bound for \(\mathcal I\) under \(H\) if the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm that, on every \(n\)-bit instance \(I\in\mathcal I\), returns feasible \(x\) satisfying \(f_I(x)\le r(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) would contradict \(H\). An approximation threshold additionally identifies an attainable factor \(u(n)\) and a forbidden factor \(r(n)\), with the gap and all strict or asymptotic conventions stated explicitly. The class \(\mathcal I\), objective normalization, input encoding, factors, and assumption \(H\) are part of the claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inapproximability bound forbids a specified approximation factor under a named complexity assumption; a threshold also states the attainable side and any gap between the two sides.
assumptions_latex: \(f_I(x)\ge0\) for feasible \(x\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
\(H\) is an explicit complexity assumption.
Input length \(n\) and the instance class \(\mathcal I\) are fixed by the claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forbidden factor \(r(n)\) and any attainable factor \(u(n)\) are meaningful only relative to \(\mathcal I\), its encoding, and \(H\).

notation.meaning: factor ruled out by the hardness result
factor achieved by an approximation algorithm when an attainable side is stated
complexity assumption supporting the lower bound

children.title: Restriction-Dependent Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation behavior enabled by structural, dimensional, or domain restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-Dependent Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantees remain conditional on the structural restrictions used by their algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I_R\subseteq\mathcal I\) be the instances satisfying a restriction \(R\), such as fixed dimension, bounded coefficients, sparsity, or a special quadratic structure. If algorithm \(A\) is polynomial-time and satisfies \(f_I(A(I))\le\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) only for \(I\in\mathcal I_R\), then its approximation guarantee is a property of the pair \((\mathcal I_R,A)\). It does not imply the same runtime or factor on \(\mathcal I\setminus\mathcal I_R\). Removing \(R\) requires an independent analysis because feasibility, relaxation quality, or enumeration size may change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximation ratio proved under fixed dimension, bounded data, sparsity, or special structure does not automatically extend when that restriction is removed.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I_R\subseteq\mathcal I\).
The runtime and ratio analysis of \(A\) uses restriction \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factor \(\rho(n)\) is established only on \(\mathcal I_R\), not automatically on all of \(\mathcal I\).

source_refs.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

children.title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability
children.top_down_role: Global optimization regimes controlled by a designated structural or dimensional parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized runtime criterion for a fixed exact or accuracy-qualified global MICP computational task.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a parameterized computational task \(Q\) for nonconvex MICP, such as exact global solution or solution to a specified \(\varepsilon\)-global criterion. For an encoded instance \(I\) of length \(n=|I|\), including the encoded accuracy requirement when it is part of the task, let \(k(I)\in\mathbb N\) be a computable parameter. The task \(Q\) is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to \(k\) if an algorithm solves every instance in time \(g(k(I))n^c\), where \(g\) is computable and the constant \(c\) is independent of \(k(I)\). A runtime of the form \(n^{g(k(I))}\) establishes at most XP membership in general, not fixed-parameter tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed exact or approximation task is fixed-parameter tractable when all unrestricted parameter dependence lies outside a constant input-length exponent; accuracy data must be included in the encoded task.
assumptions_latex: The computational task \(Q\) and its output criterion are fixed before classifying its complexity.
\(n=|I|\) includes every encoded part of the task, including an accuracy request when applicable.
\(k(I)\) is explicitly defined and computable from \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: FPT requires runtime \(g(k(I))n^c\) with \(c\) independent of \(k(I)\); a bound \(n^{g(k(I))}\) is generally only XP.

notation.meaning: length of the complete encoded instance

children.title: Bounded-Domain Tractability
children.top_down_role: Complexity improvements attributable to finite or quantitatively bounded variable domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-grid additive approximation on bounded mixed continuous-integer product domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D>0\), \(L>0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), \(X=[0,D]^d\), and let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) be explicitly enumerable with \(|Z|=M\). Suppose \(f:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(|f(x,z)-f(y,z)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\) for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(z\in Z\). Set \(m=\lceil LD/\varepsilon\rceil\) and evaluate every \(z\in Z\) and every point of the grid \(\{0,D/m,2D/m,\ldots,D\}^d\). A best evaluated pair \((\hat x,\hat z)\) satisfies \[f(\hat x,\hat z)\le\min_{(x,z)\in X\times Z}f(x,z)+\varepsilon.\] The number of evaluations is at most \(M(1+\lceil LD/\varepsilon\rceil)^d\), which is polynomial in \(M\) and \(1/\varepsilon\) for fixed \(d\) and fixed encoded \(L,D\), but exponential in variable \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded product domain, an explicitly defined uniform grid gives additive Lipschitz approximation with the stated evaluation count; polynomial dependence requires fixed continuous dimension and controlled domain data.
assumptions_latex: \(D>0\), \(L>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
\(X=[0,D]^d\), and \(Z\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) is explicitly enumerable with \(|Z|=M<\infty\).
\(|f(x,z)-f(y,z)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\) for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(z\in Z\).
Objective evaluations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(M(1+\lceil LD/\varepsilon\rceil)^d\) evaluations suffice for additive error at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: positive Lipschitz constant in the continuous variables
number of explicitly enumerable integer assignments
number of equal grid intervals per continuous coordinate

children.title: Parameter-Domain Interaction
children.top_down_role: Tractability regimes requiring simultaneous control of selected parameters plus domain extent.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Domain Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How domain bounds alter the parameterized complexity of integer enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a MICP has \(k\) integer variables, each ranging over at most \(B+1\) values, and each fixed-integer continuous subproblem costs \(T(n)\). Complete integer enumeration costs at most
\[(B+1)^kT(n).\]
If both \(k\) and \(B\) are parameters and \(T(n)\) is polynomial, this is fixed-parameter tractable in \((k,B)\). If only \(k\) is parameterized while \(B\) may grow with the binary input, the same bound does not establish FPT in \(k\); when \(B\) is polynomial in \(n\), it generally has XP form \(n^{O(k)}T(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration is FPT when integer dimension and domain size are parameters, but varying encoded bounds can turn the same method into XP.
assumptions_latex: There are \(k\) integer variables with at most \(B+1\) values each.
Every fixed-integer continuous subproblem is solved in time \(T(n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumeration costs \((B+1)^kT(n)\), giving FPT in \((k,B)\) but not necessarily in \(k\) alone.

source_refs.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

children.title: Unbounded-Domain Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of restricted-regime complexity guarantees when essential domain bounds are absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Domain Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite-domain enumeration when integer variables lack valid instance-dependent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Finite-domain enumeration does not extend to an unbounded integer variable without a valid truncation bound. For the one-variable family
\[\min_{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}(z-N)^2,\]
where \(N\) is a nonnegative integer encoded in binary, the unique optimizer is \(z=N\). Any enumeration restricted a priori to \(0\le z\le B\) fails whenever \(N>B\). Thus no bound independent of the instance data can make enumeration exhaustive. Moreover, enumerating through \(N\) takes \(\Omega(N)\) trials, which is exponential in the bit length \(\Theta(\log(N+1))\). Unboundedness therefore invalidates bounded-domain complexity conclusions unless coercivity or analytic bounds produce a suitably encoded finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a valid data-dependent bound, integer enumeration is incomplete; even enumeration up to a binary-encoded optimizer can be exponential in input length.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is represented in binary.
The method inspects integer points sequentially up to a truncation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No instance-independent truncation is exhaustive, and sequential enumeration may require \(\Omega(N)=2^{\Omega(\log(N+1))}\) trials.

notation.meaning: binary-encoded location of the unique optimizer

source_refs.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

children.title: Sparsity-Induced Tractability
children.top_down_role: Complexity reductions associated with sparse variable interactions or sparse constraint incidence.

assumptions_latex: The discretized node subproblem has finite variable domains of cardinality at most \(D\).
Its objective and feasibility indicator factor into \(m\) functions whose primal graph has treewidth \(\tau\).
A local factor value is computed in time at most \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{time}=O(mD^{\tau+1}T)\) and \(\operatorname{memory}=O(mD^\tau)\).

notation.meaning: treewidth of the primal interaction graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain sparse relaxations or discretized subproblems arising inside global MICP algorithms.

source_refs.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite-domain global-optimization node problem factor over a primal graph admitting a tree decomposition of width \(\tau\). Assign every factor to a bag containing its scope. Dynamic programming from the leaves to a root stores, for each separator assignment, the best feasible objective contribution in the processed subtree; an infeasible assignment receives value \(+\infty\). Combining child tables and eliminating variables local to each bag yields the exact node optimum. Since a bag contains at most \(\tau+1\) variables, the resulting bounds are \[\operatorname{time}=O(mD^{\tau+1}T),\qquad \operatorname{memory}=O(mD^\tau).\] Thus bounded treewidth and bounded domain size make this subproblem polynomial in \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorized finite-domain node problem is exactly solvable by tree-decomposition dynamic programming, with exponential dependence confined to treewidth and domain size.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity-Induced Tractability

source_witnesses.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical role and local scope fit the leaf, but the cited global-optimization survey page is not sufficiently targeted to verify the exact treewidth dynamic-programming time and memory bounds.

children.title: Decomposition-Induced Tractability
children.top_down_role: Complexity reductions arising from separable blocks, linking structure, or decomposable subproblems.

assumptions_latex: The node problem decomposes into local factors indexed by a tree decomposition.
Every separator state belongs to a finite set \(S_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root message minimum equals the exact optimum of the decomposed node problem.

notation.meaning: message from bag t to its parent p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact message-passing decomposition for finite separator states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rooted tree decomposition with local objective terms assigned to bags and finite separator-state sets. For each leaf-to-root edge \(t\to p\), compute \[M_{t\to p}(s)=\min\left\{f_t(x_{B_t})+\sum_{u\in\operatorname{ch}(t)}M_{u\to t}(x_{S_{ut}}):x_{S_{tp}}=s,\ x_{B_t}\text{ is locally feasible}\right\}.\] Store an attaining local assignment whenever the minimum is finite. At the root \(r\), minimize its local objective plus all incoming messages. If every root value is \(+\infty\), report infeasibility; otherwise backtrack stored assignments to return a globally compatible optimizer and its exact objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate decomposed blocks by separator-state messages, minimize at the root, and backtrack stored choices to recover an exact optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Induced Tractability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is coherent and fits decomposition-induced tractability, but its exactness and backtracking claims require a source specifically covering junction-tree or tree-decomposition dynamic programming.

children.title: Sparse Decomposition Coupling
children.top_down_role: Regimes where sparsity patterns determine the effectiveness of decomposition.

assumptions_latex: The formulation has variables \(V\) and factor scopes \(E\subseteq 2^V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sparse decomposability holds when \(\max_t|B_t|-1\leq\tau\) for a moderate parameter \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition linking sparse factor scopes to exact decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factorized MICP node formulation has sparse decomposition coupling of width at most \(\tau\) if there is a tree \(\mathcal T\) with bags \(B_t\subseteq V\) such that: \(\bigcup_{t\in\mathcal T}B_t=V\); every factor scope \(e\in E\) is contained in some bag; for each variable \(i\in V\), the set \(\{t:i\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree; and \(\max_{t\in\mathcal T}|B_t|-1\leq\tau\). The intersections \(B_t\cap B_u\) on tree edges are then the only states through which adjacent decomposed blocks must coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse decomposition coupling means all factor scopes fit in small tree-decomposition bags and each shared variable satisfies the running-intersection property.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Decomposition Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard tree-decomposition condition and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports its application to the stated factorized MICP setting.

children.title: Dense-Coupling Tractability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of structural tractability when dense global coupling defeats sparse or decomposable organization.

assumptions_latex: Finite-domain factors have domain size \(D\geq2\).
Every admissible decomposition has width \(\tau_n\geq cn\) for some constant \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard bag-enumeration bound is \(D^{\Omega(n)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific boundary for exact tree-decomposition dynamic programming.

source_refs.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact dynamic programming that enumerates assignments on decomposition bags, a width-\(\tau_n\) formulation requires tables containing up to \(D^{\tau_n+1}\) entries. Consequently, if dense global coupling forces \(\tau_n\geq cn\) with fixed \(c>0\) and \(D\geq2\), then \[D^{\tau_n+1}\geq D^{cn}=D^{\Omega(n)}.\] Bounded-width tractability therefore ends when the minimum usable decomposition width grows linearly with problem size. This conclusion is a boundary for bag-enumeration decomposition methods; it does not assert that every possible algorithm is exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When dense coupling forces decomposition width to grow linearly, exact bag-enumeration dynamic programming requires exponentially large tables.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Coupling Tractability Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: Complexity Issues in Global Optimization: A Survey p. 27

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary is correctly limited to bag-enumeration dynamic programming, but the cited survey locator does not clearly support the decomposition-width table-size claim.

children.title: Oracle-Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Computational regimes distinguished by the expense of separation, bounding, or conic certification oracles.

assumptions_latex: Each oracle \(O_i\) is called on an input of encoded size \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are classified by the asymptotic growth of \(C_i(n)\).

notation.meaning: worst-case cost of one oracle call

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-call computational regimes, excluding the number of search-tree calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an oracle \(O_i\), let \(C_i(n)\) be the worst-case arithmetic or bit-operation cost of one call on an input of encoded size \(n\). Its oracle-cost regime is called polynomial when \(C_i(n)\leq n^{O(1)}\); fixed-parameter tractable with parameter \(k\) when \(C_i(n,k)\leq f(k)n^{O(1)}\) for a computable function \(f\); subexponential when \(C_i(n)=2^{o(n)}\); and exponential when \(C_i(n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\). Total algorithmic cost additionally multiplies or aggregates these per-call costs over all visited nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-cost regimes classify the worst-case expense of one call as polynomial, parameterized, subexponential, or exponential in encoded input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the proposed polynomial, parameterized, subexponential, and exponential labels are not mutually exclusive and no source specifies how these oracle-cost regimes are intended to be used.

children.title: Relaxation-Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by lower-bound quality, feasible-region contraction, or certification power.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with node optimum \(v\).
A baseline lower bound satisfies \(L_0<v\), and oracle bounds satisfy \(L_i\leq v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strength is measured by \(\rho_i=(L_i-L_0)/(v-L_0)\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized lower-bound strength for minimization nodes with finite baseline gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization node with finite optimum \(v\), baseline lower bound \(L_0<v\), and valid oracle lower bound \(L_i\leq v\), define \[\rho_i=\frac{L_i-L_0}{v-L_0}.\] An improving valid relaxation has \(0\leq\rho_i\leq1\). Along a family indexed by size \(n\), the oracle is asymptotically weak when \(\rho_i(n)\to0\), constant-strength when \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\rho_i(n)>0\), and asymptotically exact when \(\rho_i(n)\to1\). These regimes compare bound closure, not runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation strength is the fraction of the baseline optimality gap closed by a valid lower bound, with weak, constant, and asymptotically exact regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Strength Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized gap-closure formula is mathematically coherent, including its restriction to improving bounds, but the asymptotic regime terminology and thresholds lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Cost-Strength Efficiency Frontier
children.top_down_role: Comparative regimes balancing oracle expense against resulting relaxation improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Strength Efficiency Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier for per-call cost and residual node gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization node with finite optimum \(v\), associate oracle \(i\) with \((C_i,G_i)\), where \(C_i>0\) is its per-call cost, \(L_i\leq v\) is its valid lower bound, and \(G_i=v-L_i\geq0\) is its residual gap. Oracle \(j\) dominates oracle \(i\) when \(C_j\leq C_i\) and \(G_j\leq G_i\), with at least one inequality strict. The cost-strength efficiency frontier is \[\mathcal F=\left\{i:\nexists j\text{ with }C_j\leq C_i,\ G_j\leq G_i,\text{ and }(C_j,G_j)\neq(C_i,G_i)\right\}.\] If a scalar criterion \(\Phi(C,G)\) strictly increases whenever one coordinate increases and the other does not decrease, then every oracle minimizing \(\Phi(C_i,G_i)\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle is on the cost-strength efficiency frontier exactly when no other oracle is no more costly and has no larger residual gap, with at least one strict improvement. Every optimizer of a criterion that strictly penalizes such dominance lies on this frontier.
assumptions_latex: The node is a minimization problem with finite optimum \(v\).
Each oracle has per-call cost \(C_i>0\) and returns a valid lower bound \(L_i\leq v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle \(i\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\) exactly when no \(j\) satisfies \(C_j\leq C_i\) and \(v-L_j\leq v-L_i\), with at least one strict inequality.

children.title: Oracle-Dominance Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where added relaxation strength fails to offset oracle or relaxation-solving cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Dominance Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise boundary between universal dominance and instance-dependent tradeoffs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a nonempty instance class \(\mathcal I\), oracle \(j\) universally dominates oracle \(i\) when \(C_j(I)\leq C_i(I)\) and \(L_j(I)\geq L_i(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), with at least one of these inequalities strict for at least one instance. The oracle-dominance boundary between \(i\) and \(j\) is mutual nondominance: there is an instance \(I\in\mathcal I\) for which \(C_j(I)>C_i(I)\) or \(L_j(I)<L_i(I)\), and there is an instance \(I'\in\mathcal I\), possibly equal to \(I\), for which \(C_i(I')>C_j(I')\) or \(L_i(I')<L_j(I')\). Beyond this boundary, cost and bound strength alone yield no universal dominance ordering between the two oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal dominance requires an oracle to be no more costly and no weaker on every instance, with a strict advantage somewhere. The dominance boundary is mutual nondominance, which may arise from opposing cost and strength comparisons even on one instance.
assumptions_latex: Oracle comparisons use the same nonempty instance class \(\mathcal I\) and computational model.
Each \(L_i(I)\) is a valid lower bound for the same minimization problem, so larger values are stronger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle \(j\) universally dominates oracle \(i\) exactly when \(C_j(I)\leq C_i(I)\) and \(L_j(I)\geq L_i(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), with at least one strict inequality for at least one instance.

notation.meaning: cost of oracle i on instance I
valid lower bound returned by oracle i on instance I

assumptions_latex: The intended set is \(K=\{(x,y,z):x^2\leq yz,\ y\geq0,\ z\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(2x\) by \(x\) yields the strict relaxation \(x^2\leq4yz\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling error in a rotated second-order-cone representation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The correct second-order-cone representation of \(K\) is \[\left\|(2x,y-z)\right\|_2\leq y+z.\] If a model instead imposes \(\left\|(x,y-z)\right\|_2\leq y+z\), squaring gives \(x^2+(y-z)^2\leq(y+z)^2\), hence \(x^2\leq4yz\). Thus \(\widehat K\) strictly contains \(K\). For example, \((x,y,z)=(2,1,1)\) belongs to \(\widehat K\) because \(2\leq2\), but it does not belong to \(K\) because \(4>1\). The incorrect conic scaling therefore invalidates any global bound derived from equivalence with \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing factor of two in the rotated-cone norm changes the intended product inequality and admits points that violate the original constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Incorrect Conic Representation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and cone scaling are mathematically correct and fit the failure leaf, but the cited general chapter locator does not clearly document the rotated-cone convention or this representation error.

assumptions_latex: A bilinear term satisfies \(w=xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite valid bounds are required before finite McCormick inequalities can be asserted globally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for bound-dependent bilinear relaxations.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3
Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The four McCormick inequalities for \(w=xy\) are valid on the box \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\) only when all four bounds are finite and valid for every feasible point. If a claimed bound excludes a feasible value, the resulting relaxation can exclude the original graph. For example, using \(0\leq x,y\leq1\) gives \(w\geq x+y-1\). The original graph point \((x,y,w)=(2,0,0)\) violates this inequality. If a bound is missing or infinite, the corresponding finite-coefficient McCormick inequality is undefined rather than globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound-dependent bilinear envelopes require finite valid bounds; false bounds can remove feasible graph points, while missing bounds make finite envelope coefficients unavailable.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Invalid Variable Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3
Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

assumptions_latex: The inequality \(w\geq x+y-1\) is taken from the McCormick envelope on \([0,1]^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: That inequality is invalid for the graph \(w=xy\) on any domain containing \((2,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Using a valid envelope outside the domain from which it was derived.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(B=[0,1]^2\), the McCormick inequality \(w\geq x+y-1\) is valid for \(w=xy\). Let the actual domain be \(D=[0,2]\times[0,1]\). The graph point \((x,y,w)=(2,0,0)\in G_D\) satisfies \(w=xy\), but the imported inequality requires \(0\geq1\), which is false. Hence an envelope derived for \(B\) is not automatically valid on the larger domain \(D\). A global MICP relaxation using it without enforcing \((x,y)\in B\) may cut off feasible solutions and produce an invalid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A McCormick inequality valid on the unit box can cut off bilinear graph points when reused on a larger variable domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Mismatched Envelopes

assumptions_latex: The closed perspective is formed from \(f(u)=e^u\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure error at zero activation for a noncoercive convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z>0\), consider the perspective epigraph \(t\geq z e^{x/z}\). Its lower-semicontinuous closure at \(z=0\) is governed by the recession function of \(f(u)=e^u\): it equals \(0\) for directions \(x\leq0\) and \(+\infty\) for \(x>0\). Therefore \[P\cap\{z=0\}=\{(x,0,t):x\leq0,\ t\geq0\}.\] The commonly imposed rule \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\) is strictly stronger: \((-1,0,0)\) belongs to the true closed perspective epigraph but violates that rule. An unsupported zero-activation convention can therefore remove valid closure points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the exponential perspective, the true zero-activation closure permits every nonpositive scaled argument; forcing the argument to zero is invalidly restrictive.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Perspective Closures

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone and \(H=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\). The conic system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is weakly infeasible when \(H\cap K=\varnothing\) but \[\operatorname{dist}(H,K)=\inf\{\|h-k\|_2:h\in H,\ k\in K\}=0.\] Thus no feasible point exists, yet every positive separation tolerance admits \(h\in H\) and \(k\in K\) with \(\|h-k\|_2\) below that tolerance; consequently, no strict separating hyperplane certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is weakly infeasible when its affine constraints and cone do not intersect but have zero distance, preventing strict separation certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex cone.
\(H=\{x:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(H,K)=0\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance between the two sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-distance definition is standard, but the claim about absence of a strict separating certificate depends on the precise separation convention and requires an authoritative conic-feasibility source.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive value gap for a primal-dual conic pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and dual problem \(d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y\in K^*\}\), weak duality gives \(d^*\le p^*\). A finite positive conic duality gap occurs when both values are finite and \(d^*<p^*\). Therefore a dual feasible value remains a valid lower bound for minimization, but it cannot certify primal optimality at \(p^*\). Slater-type regularity excludes this pathology in standard finite-dimensional closed-cone formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic duality gap is the strict difference between finite primal and dual optimal values; dual bounds remain valid but cannot certify the primal optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex cone.
The primal and dual optimal values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*<p^*\) characterizes a positive duality gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal or Dual Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite conic value without an optimizing feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible set \(P\) and objective \(f\), primal nonattainment means \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) while \(f(x)>p^*\) for every \(x\in P\). For its maximization dual with feasible set \(D\) and objective \(g\), dual nonattainment means \(d^*=\sup_{y\in D}g(y)\in\mathbb{R}\) while \(g(y)<d^*\) for every \(y\in D\). Nonattainment may occur even when \(p^*=d^*\), so equality of values alone does not supply primal or dual optimizer certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonattainment occurs when a finite primal infimum or dual supremum exists but no feasible point realizes that value, possibly even with zero duality gap.
assumptions_latex: The relevant feasible set is nonempty.
The relevant optimal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No feasible primal or dual point realizes its corresponding optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Cone-Face Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic degeneracy caused by confinement to a proper face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Cone-face degeneracy occurs when the minimal face \(F\) of \(K\) containing \(S\) is proper, \(F\subsetneq K\); equivalently, feasibility is confined to the boundary geometry and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\). Interior-point regularity over \(K\) then fails. Dual attainment, strict complementarity, or exposing certificates cannot be inferred without additional assumptions; replacing \(K\) by \(F\) through facial reduction restores the appropriate relative-interior formulation when \(F\) is identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-face degeneracy occurs when every feasible point lies in a proper face of the cone, invalidating interior regularity and potentially obstructing standard dual certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
\(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimal face \(F\) containing \(S\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq K\), hence \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of K containing S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is plausible, but the minimal-face equivalence and the claimed restoration through facial reduction require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Factor-Domain Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finite factor envelopes on unbounded domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a lifted bilinear equality \(w=xy\) over a factor domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\). Standard McCormick inequalities require finite bounds \(\ell_x\le x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le y\le u_y\). If any required bound is infinite, the corresponding affine envelope has nonfinite coefficients and does not define that relaxation. Omitting such inequalities leaves a relaxation whose projection may admit arbitrary inconsistent triples \((x,y,w)\). Consequently, spatial refinement of other variables need not close the lower-bound gap unless finite local factor bounds or another valid convexification are established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bilinear envelope relaxations can remain arbitrarily weak when a factor lacks finite bounds, because the required McCormick inequalities are unavailable.
assumptions_latex: The formulation contains \(w=xy\).
At least one factor lacks a finite lower or upper bound required by the envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard four-inequality McCormick relaxation is unavailable or incomplete and need not converge under unrelated branching.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Finite factor bounds are required for the standard four McCormick inequalities, but the broader claims about arbitrary inconsistent triples and stagnation under unrelated branching need sourced qualifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Gap Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent non-rank-one solutions in lifted relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a nonconvex model imposes \(X=xx^\top\), while its convex relaxation retains only \(X-xx^\top\succeq0\). At relaxation level \(k\), let \((x_k,X_k)\) be optimal and define \(r_k=\operatorname{rank}(X_k- x_kx_k^\top)\). Rank-gap stagnation occurs when the relaxation lower bounds \(L_k\) fail to reach a known feasible value \(U\) and \(r_k>0\) persists along the refinement sequence. The relaxed solutions then do not satisfy the lifted equality, so neither feasibility recovery nor global gap closure follows from solving additional unchanged-rank relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-gap stagnation means lifted relaxations retain nonzero rank residuals while their lower bounds stay below the incumbent, preventing recovery of the original factorization.
assumptions_latex: The original model requires \(X=xx^\top\).
Each relaxation enforces \(X-xx^\top\succeq0\).
A finite feasible incumbent value \(U\) is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent \(r_k>0\) and \(L_k<U\) prevent certification through the stated relaxation sequence.

notation.meaning: Relaxation lower bound and feasible incumbent value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-rank condition is coherent, but “rank-gap stagnation” is not standardized and the conclusion depends on how the refinement sequence changes the relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Activation Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gap from relaxed on-off indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\) activate a set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with feasible disjunction \(S=(\{0\}\times\{0\})\cup(D\times\{1\})\) in variables \((x,z)\). A continuous activation formulation \(R\) is fractionally weak when \(S\subseteq R\), \(R\) permits \(0<z<1\), and \(R\supsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\). Then some linear objective separates a point of \(R\) from \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\), producing a strict relaxation gap. Branching only on unrelated variables cannot remove that fractional activation point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An on-off relaxation is fractionally weak when it contains fractional indicator points outside the closed convex hull of the intended disjunction, creating a linear-objective gap.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a closed convex relaxation containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\supsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\) implies a strict relaxation gap for some linear objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Strict containment of the closed convex hull supports a separating linear objective in finite dimensions, but persistence under branching on “unrelated” variables is not formally specified or sourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation-Induced Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict weakening caused by aggregating valid constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(g_i(x)\le0\), every nonnegative aggregation \(\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le0\), with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), is implied by the original system, so \[\{x:g_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\}\subseteq\left\{x:\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le0\right\}.\] Inclusion can be strict: the pair \(x\le0\) and \(-x\le0\) yields only \(x=0\), whereas equal positive weights produce the tautology \(0\le0\), admitting every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Replacing the disaggregated constraints by this aggregate therefore destroys all bounding strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative constraint aggregation is generally weaker than the original system; equal aggregation of x≤0 and −x≤0 becomes a tautology.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every aggregated inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregation preserves validity but can strictly enlarge the relaxation feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexhaustive Spatial Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search invalidity when children do not cover their parent region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a live node represent a region \(R\), let \(F\) be the original feasible set, and let branching create child regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\). Branching is exhaustive on feasible parent points if \[F\cap R\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^m R_j.\] If this inclusion fails, the omitted set \[(F\cap R)\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^m R_j\] contains a feasible point and may contain a global optimizer. If the parent is removed without a separate valid fathoming certificate for the omitted set, bounds over the children alone do not certify a global bound over \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spatial branching is nonexhaustive when its children omit feasible parent points. Removing the parent without separately certifying the omitted set can discard a global optimizer, and child bounds alone then cannot certify the parent region.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the original feasible set.
\(R\) is a live node region.
\(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) are the generated child regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F\cap R\nsubseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^mR_j\), removing the parent is uncertified unless the omitted feasible set is separately and validly fathomed.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Node Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invalid lower bounds in a minimization search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization node with region \(R_N\), a valid node lower bound \(L_N\) must satisfy \(L_N\le f_N^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap R_N\}\), using the same objective scale and conventions as the incumbent. A node bound is inconsistent when \(L_N>f_N^*\). If such a node is pruned because \(L_N\ge U\), where \(U\) is a feasible incumbent value, the node may still contain a point better than \(U\); hence the pruning decision and any global optimality gap derived from it are invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization node bound is inconsistent when it exceeds the node’s true infimum; pruning with it can discard solutions better than the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the objective value of a feasible incumbent.
\(F\cap R_N\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_N>f_N^*\) makes bound-based pruning at node \(N\) unsound.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Local-Cut Inheritance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applying a locally valid cut outside its validity region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a cut \(a^\top x\le\beta\) be valid only on a region \(V\), meaning \(F\cap V\subseteq\{x:a^\top x\le\beta\}\). Adding it at a node with region \(R_N\) is safe only if \(F\cap R_N\subseteq V\), or if validity on \(F\cap R_N\) is separately established. If the cut is inherited by a node violating this condition, some feasible point in that node may be removed. Any lower bound, pruning decision, or optimality certificate obtained from the cut-restricted node is then not valid for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local cut is unsafe when inherited by a node outside its proven validity region, because it may exclude feasible points and corrupt bounds or pruning.
assumptions_latex: The cut is known valid on \(F\cap V\).
No global validity outside \(V\) is established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inheritance is uncertified whenever \(F\cap R_N\nsubseteq V\) and node-specific validity is absent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The safety condition is mathematically plausible and appropriately qualified by separately established node validity, but no source supports the local-cut inheritance claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Gap Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination based on an uncertified global optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(U\) be the value of a certified feasible incumbent, let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the active-node set, and let each \(L_N\) be a valid lower bound for active node \(N\). Assume every feasible point outside the active-node regions has been validly fathomed at objective value at least \(U\). With \[L=\min_{N\in\mathcal{A}}L_N,\] a sound absolute-gap test is \(U-L\le\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Gap closure is premature when this test is declared without certified incumbent feasibility, valid node bounds, exhaustive active-node coverage together with valid prior fathoming, or a consistently defined gap calculation. Under such a failure, the reported gap is not justified as a bound on \(U-f^*\), where \(f^*\) is the global infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute gap test is globally valid only when the incumbent is feasible, active-node bounds are valid, and all feasible regions outside the active nodes have been safely fathomed. Otherwise gap closure is premature and the reported gap is not a justified global-suboptimality bound.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) is the absolute optimality tolerance.
Every feasible point outside the active-node regions has a valid fathoming certificate at value at least \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without incumbent feasibility, valid node bounds, and exhaustive coverage or valid fathoming of all feasible regions, \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) is not a justified global certificate.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound for active node N

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational dominance is defined by the measured fraction of branch-and-bound cost spent solving node relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), relaxation-cost dominance holds when
\[
D_R:=\frac{\sum_{v\in V}r_v}{\sum_{v\in V}(r_v+a_v+o_v)}\ge 1-\varepsilon.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{\sum_{v\in V}(a_v+o_v)}{\sum_{v\in V}(r_v+a_v+o_v)}\le\varepsilon.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation-cost dominance means that solving node relaxations consumes at least a prescribed fraction of total run cost, equivalently leaving at most the complementary fraction for audits and other work.
assumptions_latex: A global MICP run processes nodes \(v\in V\).
Each node incurs relaxation cost \(r_v\ge 0\), audit cost \(a_v\ge 0\), and other cost \(o_v\ge 0\).
The total measured cost \(\sum_{v\in V}(r_v+a_v+o_v)\) is positive.
The threshold satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_R\ge 1-\varepsilon\), and the non-relaxation fraction is at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation, audit, and other costs at node v.
Fraction of total measured cost spent solving relaxations.
